summary: Defines methodologies for benchmarking the control-plane performance of SDN controllers, which are implemented with many different designs. It describes how to run comparable tests so results can be understood across controllers.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook for a fair race between network controllers, so everyone is timed the same way.

questions: how to test sdn controller performance
subtitle: How to fairly measure and compare Software-Defined Networking controller performance.

tldr.problem: SDN controllers are implemented very differently—some prioritize speed, some prioritize scalability, some optimize for reliability. Comparing two controllers' performance is difficult because there is no standard way to test them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a black-box benchmarking methodology treating any SDN controller as a device with a control plane (receiving commands from applications) and a forwarding plane (controlling network devices). It specifies a common test lab setup, repeatable test procedures, and metrics for performance (latency, throughput), scalability (how many devices and flows), reliability (failover time), and security (exception handling).
tldr.outcome: Network operators and engineers can now run the same tests on different controllers and compare results fairly. The RFC covers both standalone and clustered controller setups and includes an appendix with examples using OpenFlow, a popular SDN protocol.

today: RFC 8456 is an Informational RFC published in October 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the standard benchmark methodology for SDN controller testing and is widely used by vendors and operators to compare controller performance fairly.

sections.title: Why Benchmark SDN Controllers?
sections.content: Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is an architecture where a central controller program tells network devices (switches, routers) what to do via APIs instead of each device making its own decisions. A controller is the "brain." Different vendors and teams have built controllers in completely different ways: some in Java, some in Python, some in C; some with clustered redundancy, some standalone; some optimized for speed, some for handling millions of flows. To choose a controller for a network, operators need to know not just features but performance. This RFC provides a methodology so that performance claims are backed by repeatable tests anyone can run and verify.
sections.eli5: If you are choosing a network brain for your company, you want to know how fast it thinks, how many devices it can manage, and whether it stays calm when things go wrong—just like interviewing a manager.

sections.title: The Test Setup
sections.content: The RFC defines a lab test setup using a black-box model: the controller under test (called the Device Under Test or DUT) is in the middle. Above it, an Application-Plane Test Emulator simulates applications making requests (north interface). Below it, a Forwarding-Plane Test Emulator simulates network devices like switches responding to the controller (south interface). The emulator timestamps control messages to measure latency and count message rates. The test topology should use a realistic Leaf-Spine architecture with at least two simulated network devices. Tests can be run in two modes: a single standalone controller, or a cluster of identical controllers with East-West (controller-to-controller) coordination. This setup is hardware-agnostic: the controller can be a physical server or a virtual machine, and tests measure performance independently of which southbound protocol (OpenFlow, NETCONF, etc.) the controller uses.
sections.eli5: The test is like putting the controller in a box with pretend applications above it and pretend network devices below it, measuring every message and how long it takes to respond.

sections.title: Test Conditions and Reporting
sections.content: The RFC specifies test conditions to ensure repeatable results: test traffic uses frame sizes of 128, 512, and 1508 bytes (and optional jumbo frames). Each test should be repeated at least 10 times. Measurement points are specified at the emulator interfaces to capture timing accurately. Connectivity should be direct (no intermediate devices introducing delay). Reports must document the controller name and version, protocols used, whether the setup is standalone or clustered, encryption yes/no, the network topology (nodes and links), test traffic types, and the controller system configuration (CPU, memory, operating system, storage). The RFC also recommends specifying controller settings like topology rediscovery timeout and whether controller state is persisted (saved to disk for recovery after a crash). Test emulator capabilities must be reported: the maximum number of devices it can simulate and its own message processing time.
sections.eli5: Just like a science experiment, you have to write down exactly what you tested, what hardware you used, and repeat the test many times so others can believe your results.

sections.title: Performance Metrics: Speed and Throughput
sections.content: The RFC defines eight performance tests. Network Topology Discovery Time measures how long the controller takes to learn the layout of the network from discovery messages from switches. Asynchronous Message Processing Time measures the round-trip time for the controller to process a single message from a switch (e.g., "a new flow arrived") and send a response. Asynchronous Message Processing Rate measures how many such messages per second the controller can handle before it starts dropping them or falling behind. Reactive Path Provisioning Time measures the time to set up a path through the network in response to a new flow request. Proactive Path Provisioning Time measures the time to set up a path by pushing rules in advance before any flow arrives. Reactive and Proactive Path Provisioning Rate measure throughput for each mode. Network Topology Change Detection Time measures how quickly the controller detects and responds when a link fails or changes. Each metric is measured multiple times, and results report average and variance to quantify consistency.
sections.eli5: These tests ask: How fast does the controller learn the network? How many messages per second can it handle? How long to set up a new path? If a link breaks, how fast does it notice?

sections.title: Scalability Metrics: How Big Can It Get?
sections.content: Scalability tests push the controller to its limits. Control Sessions Capacity measures the maximum number of simultaneous connections the controller can handle (e.g., how many switches can connect at once). Network Discovery Size measures the largest network the controller can learn and manage (how many devices and links). Forwarding Table Capacity measures the maximum number of flow entries the controller can install and manage. These tests identify breaking points: at what scale does the controller's latency degrade or connections start failing? Scalability is especially important because operators may start with a small network and grow it, or deploy a controller across multiple data centers.
sections.eli5: These tests find the limits: How many switches can call at once? How big a network can it manage? How many flow rules can it remember?

sections.title: Reliability and Security Under Stress
sections.content: The RFC includes tests for Controller Failover Time: when the active controller in a cluster fails, how long until the backup takes over and traffic flows again? Network Re-provisioning Time measures how long the backup controller takes to restore all network paths after taking over. Security tests include Exception Handling: does the controller crash or gracefully handle malformed messages? Denial-of-Service Attack Handling measures whether the controller can sustain service when flooded with invalid or malicious messages, and how much the attack degrades performance. These tests reveal robustness: will the controller melt down under stress, or does it degrade gracefully?
sections.eli5: Can the controller survive a crash and hand over to backup? What happens when someone sends it garbage data or floods it with fake messages?

items.title: Topology Discovery Time
items.text: How long to learn the network topology.

items.title: Message Processing Time
items.text: Round-trip latency for a single message.

items.title: Message Processing Rate
items.text: Maximum messages per second the controller handles.

items.title: Reactive Path Setup Time
items.text: Latency to set up a path on demand.

items.title: Proactive Path Setup Time
items.text: Latency to pre-install rules before flows arrive.

items.title: Path Setup Rate
items.text: Maximum paths per second the controller provisions.

items.title: Topology Change Detection
items.text: How fast the controller notices link failures.

items.title: Failover Time
items.text: Recovery time when a controller fails.
